Of course! Merging the last two commits is a very common task in Git, usually done to clean up your commit history before sharing it. The technical term for this is "squashing" commits.

The best and most flexible way to do this is with an **interactive rebase**.

Here’s a step-by-step guide.

---

### Method 1: Interactive Rebase (Most Common & Powerful)

This method lets you a-la-carte pick, squash, edit, or reorder recent commits.

#### Step 1: Start the Interactive Rebase

To combine the last two commits, you need to tell Git you want to rebase the last 2 commits from your current position (`HEAD`).

Open your terminal and run:
```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~2
```
*   `rebase -i` stands for "interactive rebase".
*   `HEAD~2` specifies the range: from the current commit (`HEAD`) back 2 commits.

#### Step 2: Choose Which Commits to Squash

After running the command, Git will open your default text editor (like Vim or Nano) with a file that looks something like this:

```editor
pick 22a83f8 Add feature X part 1
pick 9e7c10c Fix typo in feature X

# Rebase 3d8abf1..9e7c10c onto 3d8abf1 (2 commands)
#
# Commands:
# p, pick <commit> = use commit
# r, reword <commit> = use commit, but edit the commit message
# e, edit <commit> = use commit, but stop for amending
# s, squash <commit> = use commit, but meld into previous commit
# f, fixup <commit> = like "squash", but discard this commit's log message
# x, exec <command> = run command (the rest of the line) using shell
# b, break = stop here (continue rebase later with 'git rebase --continue')
# d, drop <commit> = remove commit
# l, label <label> = label this HEAD with a name
# t, reset <label> = reset HEAD to a label
# m, merge [-C <commit> | -c <commit>] <label> [# <oneline>]
# .       create a merge commit using the original merge commit's
# .       message (or the oneline, if no original merge commit was
# .       specified). Use -c <commit> to reword the commit message.
#
```

The commits are listed in **oldest-first** order.

To merge the second commit (`9e7c10c`) into the first one (`22a83f8`), change the word `pick` on the second line to `squash` (or just `s`).

Your file should now look like this:

```editor
pick 22a83f8 Add feature X part 1
squash 9e7c10c Fix typo in feature X
```

> **Tip:** You could also use `fixup` (or `f`) instead of `squash`.
> *   `squash`: Combines the commits and lets you edit the commit messages together.
> *   `fixup`: Combines the commits but **discards** the message of the "fixup" commit. This is great for small typo-fixes where you don't need to keep the "fixed typo" message.

Save and close the editor.

#### Step 3: Combine the Commit Messages

Next, Git will open another editor window containing the commit messages from both commits.

```editor
# This is a combination of 2 commits.
# The first line will be the subject of the new commit.

Add feature X part 1

# This is the 2nd commit message:

Fix typo in feature X
```

Now, edit this file to create the new, single, clean commit message. For example, you can just delete the second message and clean up the first one.

A good final message might be:
```editor
Add feature X
```

Save and close this editor.

#### Step 4: All Done!

Git will apply the changes, and your last two commits will be combined into one. You can verify this by looking at your log:

```bash
git log --oneline -n 3
```
You will now see one new commit where there were previously two.

---

### Method 2: Soft Reset (Simpler, but Less Flexible)

This method is quicker if all you want to do is combine the last `N` commits into one new commit, and you don't need the fine-grained control of an interactive rebase.

#### Step 1: Reset the Branch to the Correct Commit
A "soft" reset moves the `HEAD` pointer back two commits but **keeps all the changes** from those two commits in your staging area.

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~2
```

#### Step 2: Check Your Status
If you now run `git status`, you'll see that the changes from both of your last two commits are staged and ready to be committed.

```bash
git status
```
```
On branch my-feature
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   some-file.js
        new file:   another-file.py
```

#### Step 3: Create the New Commit
Now, simply create a new commit that includes all of those staged changes.

```bash
git commit -m "New combined commit message for feature X"
```
And that's it! You have successfully replaced your last two commits with a single, new one.

---

### ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Pushed vs. Unpushed Commits

This is crucial. Both of these methods **rewrite Git history**.

#### **Scenario 1: The commits have NOT been pushed to a remote repository (like GitHub).**

You are safe! This is the ideal time to clean up your history. Use either method freely.

#### **Scenario 2: The commits HAVE already been pushed.**

**Be very careful.** Rewriting history that others may have already pulled is dangerous and can create major problems for your teammates.

*   **Never do this on a shared branch** (like `main`, `master`, or `develop`) unless you are the sole contributor or have coordinated with your entire team.
*   If you've rewritten history on your own feature branch that only you are using, you will have to **force push** your changes to update the remote.

Use `--force-with-lease`, which is safer than `--force` because it won't overwrite work if someone else has pushed to the branch in the meantime.

```bash
git push --force-with-lease
```

### Summary: Which Method to Use?

| Method | Best For |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`git rebase -i`** | The standard, most powerful way. Good for squashing, but also for reordering, editing, or dropping commits. |
| **`git reset --soft`**| A quick and simple way to just combine the last N commits into one new one. |
